standard.title: Develop and Modify Inquiry Questions
standard.description: develop and modify a range of historical questions about the past to inform historical inquiry
standard.prior_knowledge: In Year 7 students developed historical questions (AC9HH7S01). In Year 8 students refined this by developing questions to inform inquiry (AC9HH8S01). Y9 extends this with the expectation that students develop a range of questions and modify them iteratively as the inquiry develops — adding the dimension of ongoing revision as evidence and understanding grows.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students develop and modify a range of historical questions about the past to inform historical inquiry, revising questions as new factors are introduced.

nodes.label: Developing a range of historical questions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop a range of historical questions — not just a single question — that require historical argument and go beyond factual recall.
nodes.minimum_width: Develop at least two distinct historical questions about a topic being studied, each requiring historical argument rather than factual recall.
nodes.typical_width: Develop a range of questions about aspects of the past that require historical argument; use historical concepts (cause, effect, change, continuity, significance, perspective) to frame questions at different levels; generate questions that could drive a sustained historical inquiry.
wider: Develop inquiry questions for contrasting topic types (e.g. a political event and a social movement) and reflect explicitly on how the choice of question shapes the scope and direction of the inquiry

Investigate how historians have framed their inquiry questions about the same event in different historical periods — examining how the questions historians ask change over time — and use this to develop stronger questions about a topic being studied
Develop a research question collaboratively and document each revision with a rationale, examining how questioning is an iterative intellectual process

response_modes.reason: Students frequently conflate historical questions with factual questions ('What happened at Gallipoli?' vs 'Why did Gallipoli become central to Australian national identity?'). Explicit modelling of what makes a question require historical argument is necessary before students can generate these independently.

success_criteria: Develops at least two historical questions that require historical argument rather than factual recall
Uses at least one historical concept (cause, effect, change, continuity, significance, or perspective) to frame a question

nodes.label: Modifying questions as inquiry develops
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can modify their inquiry questions as new factors are introduced, demonstrating that questioning is an iterative process responsive to growing understanding.
nodes.minimum_width: Modify at least one inquiry question in response to new information or a new factor introduced during research, explaining why the modification was made.
nodes.typical_width: Develop an inquiry question and refine it as further factors are introduced into the research process; modify questions using historical concepts such as cause, effect, change and continuity; demonstrate that questioning is ongoing — not a one-time step at the start of inquiry.
wider: Apply question modification across multiple inquiry contexts (different topics in the same unit) — practising the skill in varied settings to demonstrate transferability
Reflect in writing on how and why questions changed during an inquiry, documenting the thinking behind each revision — developing metacognitive awareness of the inquiry process

response_modes.reason: Applying question modification in multiple task contexts — different topics, different question types — develops the skill as a transferable habit rather than a one-off exercise.

success_criteria: Modifies at least one inquiry question in response to new information, identifying what changed and why
Demonstrates that the modified question is more precise, more arguable, or better suited to the available evidence than the original
